claim: AWS X-Ray collects data about the requests that your application serves and provides tools to view, filter and gain insights into that data to identify issues and opportunities for optimization.
q: What does AWS X-Ray do?
v: collects data about requests that your application serves
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/aws-xray

AWS X-Ray is a service that collects data about requests that your application serves, and provides tools that you can use to view, filter, and gain insights into that data to identify issues and opportunities for optimization.

claim: X-Ray receives data from services as segments, groups segments that have a common request into traces, and processes the traces to generate a service graph that gives a visual representation of your application.
q: How do segments, traces and the service graph relate in X-Ray?
v: receives data from services as segments
segments that have a common request
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts

AWS X-Ray receives data from services as *segments*. X-Ray then groups segments that have a common request into *traces*. X-Ray processes the traces to generate a *service graph* that provides a visual representation of your application.

claim: A segment can break down the work done into subsegments, which provide more granular timing information and details about the downstream calls your application made to fulfill the original request.
q: What is an X-Ray subsegment?
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts

A segment can break down the data about the work done into **subsegments**. Subsegments provide more granular timing information and details about downstream calls that your application made to fulfill the original request.

claim: For services that do not send their own segments, such as Amazon DynamoDB, X-Ray uses subsegments to generate inferred segments and downstream nodes on the trace map, so you see downstream dependencies even if they do not support tracing.
q: How does X-Ray show DynamoDB on the trace map when DynamoDB sends no segments?
v: downstream nodes on the trace map
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts

For services that don't send their own segments, like Amazon DynamoDB, X-Ray uses subsegments to generate *inferred segments* and downstream nodes on the trace map. This lets you see all of your downstream dependencies, even if they don't support tracing, or are external.

claim: A trace ID tracks the path of a request through your application, and a trace collects all the segments generated by a single request; the first supported service the request interacts with adds the trace ID header and propagates it downstream.
q: What does an X-Ray trace ID represent?
v: segments generated by a single request
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts
A **trace ID** tracks the path of a request through your application. A trace collects all the segments generated by a single request.
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts
The first supported service that the HTTP request interacts with adds a trace ID header to the request, and propagates it downstream to track the latency, disposition, and other request data.

claim: The sampling decision and trace ID are added to HTTP requests in tracing headers named X-Amzn-Trace-Id; all requests are traced up to a configurable minimum, and after that a percentage of requests are traced to avoid unnecessary cost.
q: Which HTTP header carries the X-Ray trace ID and sampling decision?
v: a percentage of requests are traced
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts

All requests are traced, up to a configurable minimum. After reaching that minimum, a percentage of requests are traced to avoid unnecessary cost. The sampling decision and trace ID are added to HTTP requests in **tracing headers** named `X-Amzn-Trace-Id`.

claim: A tracing header can originate from the X-Ray SDK, an AWS service or the client request, and your application can remove X-Amzn-Trace-Id from incoming requests to avoid issues caused by users adding trace IDs or sampling decisions.
q: Can a client influence X-Ray sampling by sending its own trace header?
v: an AWS service, or the client request
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts

A tracing header can originate from the X-Ray SDK, an AWS service, or the client request. Your application can remove `X-Amzn-Trace-Id` from incoming requests to avoid issues caused by users adding trace IDs or sampling decisions to their requests.

claim: If a load balancer or other intermediary forwards a request, X-Ray takes the client IP from the X-Forwarded-For header instead of the source IP; that recorded client IP can be forged and should not be trusted.
q: Which client IP does X-Ray record behind a load balancer, and can it be trusted?
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts

If a load balancer or other intermediary forwards a request to your application, X-Ray takes the client IP from the `X-Forwarded-For` header in the request instead of from the source IP in the IP packet. The client IP that is recorded for a forwarded request can be forged, so it should not be trusted.

claim: The X-Ray SDK applies a sampling algorithm to decide which requests get traced; the default sampling rate is conservative to avoid service charges when you get started, and you can change the default rule and add rules based on properties of the service or request.
q: Why does X-Ray sample requests instead of tracing all of them?
v: the default sampling rate is conservative
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts
To ensure efficient tracing and provide a representative sample of the requests that your application serves, the X-Ray SDK applies a **sampling** algorithm to determine which requests get traced.
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts

To avoid incurring service charges when you are getting started, the default sampling rate is conservative. You can configure X-Ray to modify the default sampling rule and configure additional rules that apply sampling based on properties of the service or request.

claim: In an X-Ray sampling rule, the reservoir is the number of requests per second that are always recorded (by default one request per second), and the rate is the percentage of additional requests beyond the reservoir that are sampled (by default five percent).
q: What are the reservoir and the rate of an X-Ray sampling rule?
v: One request per second is the *reservoir*
additional requests beyond the reservoir size
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-console-sampling

By default, the SDK records the first request each second, and five percent of any additional requests. One request per second is the *reservoir*. This ensures that at least one trace is recorded each second as long as the service is serving requests. Five percent is the *rate* at which additional requests beyond the reservoir size are sampled.

claim: If you define sampling rules in the X-Ray console and configure the SDK to read them from the X-Ray service, the service manages the reservoir for each rule and distributes it across instances, and you can change rules without deploying code; local JSON rules make each instance sample independently and need a redeploy to change.
q: Why define X-Ray sampling rules in the console instead of in a local file?
v: The service manages the reservoir for each rule
manage rules without making additional deployments
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-console-sampling

You can configure the X-Ray SDK to read sampling rules from a JSON document that you include with your code. However, when you run multiple instances of your service, each instance performs sampling independently. This causes the overall percentage of requests sampled to increase because the reservoirs of all of the instances are effectively added together. Additionally, to update local sampling rules, you must redeploy your code.
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-console-sampling
Because the rules are configured in the service, you can manage rules without making additional deployments.

claim: X-Ray sampling is parent-based: the sampling decision is made once, typically by the first X-Ray-enabled service that handles the request, and a downstream service honors a decision that already exists regardless of its own sampling rules.
q: Do sampling rules of a downstream service apply when the upstream service already decided?
v: the sampling decision is made only once
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-console-sampling

When configuring sampling rules, it is critical to understand that X-Ray sampling is "Parent-based." This means the sampling decision is made only once, typically by the first X-Ray-enabled service that handles the request (the "Root" service).
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-console-sampling
If a downstream service receives a request that already has a sampling decision from an upstream parent, it will honor that decision regardless of any of its own matching sampling rules.

claim: With X-Ray adaptive sampling you set a maximum sampling rate and X-Ray automatically adjusts within that limit, boosting sampling to capture error traces during anomalies and paying for extra sampling only when needed.
q: How does X-Ray adaptive sampling work?
v: you set a maximum sampling rate
X-Ray automatically adjusts within that limit
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-adaptive-sampling
With adaptive sampling, you set a maximum sampling rate, and X-Ray automatically adjusts within that limit.
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-adaptive-sampling
You only pay for extra sampling when needed.

claim: Adaptive sampling requires the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) SDK.
q: Which SDK does X-Ray adaptive sampling require?
v: requires the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) SDK
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-adaptive-sampling
**Supported SDK** – Adaptive sampling requires the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) SDK.

claim: In the X-Ray console you can drill down to traces for individual requests or use filter expressions to find traces related to specific paths or users.
q: How do you find the X-Ray traces for one user or URL path?
v: find traces related to specific paths or users
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts
For advanced tracing, you can drill down to traces for individual requests, or use **filter expressions** to find traces related to specific paths or users.

claim: An X-Ray group uses a filter expression to accept traces; you can call a group by name or ARN to generate its own service graph, trace summaries and CloudWatch metrics, which are published every minute.
q: What does an X-Ray group give you?
v: criteria by which to accept traces
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts
Using a filter expression, you can define criteria by which to accept traces into the group.
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts
You can call the group by name or by Amazon Resource Name (ARN) to generate its own service graph, trace summaries, and Amazon CloudWatch metrics.

claim: Updating the filter expression of an X-Ray group does not change data already recorded and applies only to subsequent traces, and groups are billed by the number of retrieved traces that match the filter expression.
q: Does changing a group's filter expression re-evaluate old traces, and how are groups billed?
v: doesn't change data that's already recorded
billed by the number of retrieved traces
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts
Updating a group's filter expression doesn't change data that's already recorded. The update applies only to subsequent traces.
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts
Groups are billed by the number of retrieved traces that match the filter expression.

claim: Annotations are simple key-value pairs that are indexed for use with filter expressions, while metadata are key-value pairs with values of any type that are not indexed and are used to store data you do not need to search on.
q: What is the difference between X-Ray annotations and metadata?
v: simple key-value pairs that are indexed
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts
**Annotations** are simple key-value pairs that are indexed for use with [filter expressions](xray-console-filters.md).
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-concepts
**Metadata** are key-value pairs with values of any type, including objects and lists, but that are not indexed.

claim: X-Ray uses trace data from AWS resources to generate a trace map showing the client, the front-end service and the backend services it calls, which you use to identify bottlenecks, latency spikes and other issues.
q: What do you use the X-Ray trace map for?
v: identify bottlenecks, latency spikes, and other issues
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/aws-xray
X-Ray uses trace data from the AWS resources that power your cloud applications to generate a detailed *trace map*.
docs/xray/latest/devguide/aws-xray
Use the trace map to identify bottlenecks, latency spikes, and other issues to solve to improve the performance of your applications.

claim: Each X-Ray client SDK sends JSON segment documents to a daemon process listening for UDP traffic instead of sending trace data directly to X-Ray; the daemon buffers segments in a queue and uploads them in batches.
q: How does trace data get from the X-Ray SDK to the X-Ray service?
v: a daemon process listening for UDP traffic
uploads them to X-Ray in batches
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/aws-xray

Instead of sending trace data directly to X-Ray, each client SDK sends JSON segment documents to a daemon process listening for UDP traffic. The [X-Ray daemon](xray-daemon.md) buffers segments in a queue and uploads them to X-Ray in batches.

claim: The AWS X-Ray daemon listens for traffic on UDP port 2000, gathers raw segment data and relays it to the X-Ray API, and it must be running so that data sent by the SDKs can reach X-Ray.
q: On which port does the X-Ray daemon listen?
v: relays it to the AWS X-Ray API
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-daemon

The AWS X-Ray daemon is a software application that listens for traffic on UDP port 2000, gathers raw segment data, and relays it to the AWS X-Ray API. The daemon works in conjunction with the AWS X-Ray SDKs and must be running so that data sent by the SDKs can reach the X-Ray service.

claim: On AWS Lambda and AWS Elastic Beanstalk you use the service's integration with X-Ray to run the daemon: Lambda runs the daemon automatically any time a function is invoked for a sampled request, and on Elastic Beanstalk you use the XRayEnabled configuration option.
q: Do you have to install the X-Ray daemon yourself on Lambda?
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-daemon

On AWS Lambda and AWS Elastic Beanstalk, use those services' integration with X-Ray to run the daemon. Lambda runs the daemon automatically any time a function is invoked for a sampled request. On Elastic Beanstalk, [use the `XRayEnabled` configuration option](xray-daemon-beanstalk.md) to run the daemon on the instances in your environment.

claim: You can install and run the X-Ray daemon on an Amazon EC2 instance with a user data script, and you use an instance profile to give the daemon permission to upload trace data to X-Ray.
q: How do you run the X-Ray daemon on EC2 and give it permissions?
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-services-ec2
You can install and run the X-Ray daemon on an Amazon EC2 instance with a user data script.
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-services-ec2
Use an instance profile to grant the daemon permission to upload trace data to X-Ray.

claim: X-Ray continuously analyzes trace data to identify emergent issues; when fault rates exceed the expected range it creates an insight that records the issue and tracks its impact until it is resolved, and insights notifications can use Amazon EventBridge.
q: How does X-Ray detect an emerging problem automatically?
v: creates an *insight* that records the issue
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-console-insights

AWS X-Ray continuously analyzes trace data in your account to identify emergent issues in your applications. When fault rates exceed the expected range, it creates an *insight* that records the issue and tracks its impact until it's resolved.
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-console-insights
Insights notifications can be integrated with your monitoring and alerting solution using Amazon EventBridge.
